candidates.title: Split text-to-SQL evaluation by database, not by example
candidates.rule: When evaluating a text-to-SQL or semantic-parsing system that is meant to work on new customer schemas, hold out entire databases (and queries) from training rather than splitting examples randomly; report the database-split number as the generalization estimate.
candidates.passage: For all models, the performance under database split is much lower than that under example split.
candidates.location: Section 8, Example Split vs Database Split (Tables 2-3)
candidates.finding: On Spider, exact-match accuracy fell sharply under database split versus example split (e.g., TypeSQL 33.0 to 8.2; SQLNet 18.3 to 12.4), and component F1 on column-bearing clauses also dropped, showing random example splits overstate cross-schema ability.
candidates.conditions: 2018-era non-pretrained parsers; values excluded from prediction (gold value lists supplied); 206 databases split 146/20/40 train/dev/test; schema names manually normalized to readable words.
candidates.limitations: Single paper, pre-LLM models; no results for modern pretrained or prompted models; database split also changes domain, so schema and domain effects are confounded; absolute numbers not transferable.
candidates.validation_test: Take a current text-to-SQL agent, evaluate it on Spider (or an internal query set) under both a random example split and a held-out-database split with matched training/few-shot budget, and compare exact-match accuracy to see whether the gap persists.

candidates.title: Expect degradation as schema foreign-key count grows
candidates.rule: When planning text-to-SQL deployments, stratify accuracy reporting by the number of foreign keys in the target schema and invest in explicit table-relation encoding or schema pruning for the high-foreign-key databases rather than assuming average accuracy holds.
candidates.passage: The performance decreases as the database has more foreign keys.
candidates.finding: Exact-match accuracy plotted against the number of foreign keys declines, which the authors attribute to larger candidate column/table sets and the need to capture inter-table relations for joins. The recommendation to add relation encoding or pruning is our extrapolation, not something they compared.
workloads: Spider exact matching accuracy as a function of foreign keys per database
candidates.conditions: Spider databases average 27.6 columns and 8.8 foreign keys; no value prediction; readable column names.
candidates.limitations: Only a trend plot, no statistics or per-bucket sample sizes; foreign-key count correlates with query difficulty, so the cause is not isolated; no intervention (relation encoding, pruning) was tested in this paper.
candidates.validation_test: Bucket Spider dev databases by foreign-key count, measure a current model's exact match per bucket, then test whether adding schema-linking/pruning or explicit foreign-key encoding closes the gap in the highest bucket.

reason: The paper is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution, but it does report controlled comparisons (example split vs database split; sketch-based vs seq2seq decoding; accuracy vs number of foreign keys) that support a few narrowly scoped evaluation and system-design rules. Rules are limited to 2018-era text-to-SQL models and Spider data.
